title: A 14-year-old female with fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, and pancytopenia: a case report
case_prompt:
A 14-year-old Middle Eastern girl presented with a 1-week history of fever, pruritic rash, anorexia, nausea, malaise, and fatigue. Four weeks earlier, she had experienced a generalized tonic–clonic seizure; brain MRI and MR venography were normal, and EEG showed epileptic waves. Phenobarbital and lamotrigine were started, with no further seizures. On admission, she was alert and oriented, with a temperature of 38.7 °C, pulse 115 beats/min, blood pressure 105/65 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. Examination revealed multiple firm, non-tender cervical and inguinal lymph nodes and an erythematous maculopapular rash on the trunk and upper limbs sparing the palms and soles, which flared with fever spikes. Cardiopulmonary, abdominal, neurologic examinations, and assessment for hepatosplenomegaly were otherwise normal.  
Laboratory studies showed pancytopenia (WBC 3.14 × 10³/μl, Hb 11.8 g/dl, platelets 118,000/mm³), elevated AST 64 IU/L, ALT 42 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 413 U/L, LDH 993 IU/L, ferritin 700 ng/ml, CRP 74 mg/dl, and ESR 13 mm/hour. Serologies were negative for EBV, CMV, and Toxoplasma IgM; HIV antibody; hepatitis B surface antigen, core antibody; and hepatitis C antibody. ANA, anti–double-stranded DNA, P-ANCA, C-ANCA, anti–liver–kidney microsomal antibodies, and rheumatoid factor were negative. Cervical ultrasound demonstrated multiple lymph nodes with preserved hilum; CT scanning of the chest and abdomen was normal except for bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. Echocardiography and ECG were normal.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Anticonvulsant hypersensitivity syndrome was the leading diagnosis given the timing of symptoms 3–4 weeks after starting phenobarbital and lamotrigine and the presence of fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, and cytopenias — “Our first diagnosis was ACHS based on fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, and pancytopenia after taking anticonvulsants.”  
2. Viral infections were considered given fever and lymphadenopathy but excluded by negative viral serologies — “viral infections … all of which were ruled out (Tables 1 and 2).”  
3. Collagen vascular disease was considered due to systemic symptoms but excluded by negative autoimmune markers — “collagen vascular disease … all of which were ruled out (Tables 1 and 2).”  
4. Hematologic malignancy was considered because of lymphadenopathy and cytopenias but excluded by normal peripheral blood smear without malignant cells — “a peripheral blood smear (PBS), which was reported by an oncologist, was normal without malignancy.”  
5. Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease was considered in an Asian adolescent with fever and cervical lymphadenopathy, but lymph‐node histopathology distinguished it from other entities — “According to symptoms, age, sex and Asian ethnicity, Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease was considered … Histopathology of the involved lymph nodes differentiated it from other diseases that it mimics.”
